title: The Great Oxidation Event, The Rusting of the Sea
description: Tonight is about air, a sea, and the colour of some very old rock. About two and a half billion years ago the air held almost none of the oxygen that most living things now depend on, and many seas held a great deal of dissolved iron. Over the following half billion years the air changed, and the rock kept the record: stripes of iron on an old sea floor, red sandstone laid down on an old land, a black stone from a lake in Karelia, and a dark shale from Gabon. It begins in the air before the change and closes on the stripes the sea left behind.

It is told through places and rock rather than through creatures, because there is almost nothing living to show: a sulphur signal in ancient sediment, a hillside of ice-scratched stone in Ontario, a field of manganese in the Kalahari, a lake in the north of Russia, and the shales of Gabon.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. When the change began (the papers put it anywhere from about 2.5 to about 2.43 billion years ago), how fast it went, whether it was one event or a long rise and fall, how early the oxygen-makers were at work, whether ice reached the equator, whether the long high in the carbon record was global, whether the structures in Gabon are early multicellular life, and what ended the iron stripes are all argued over. The popular story that oxygen poisoned most life on Earth is told near the end as a story, with what could and could not be found.
It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and no one is harmed in the telling.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the black rock at Lake Onega, that's the intended use.

accuracy: Every factual claim traces to a named source, condensed below to those the narration leans on most. Where sources disagree, the episode gives both views. Many could only be read as abstracts, summaries or digests, and a few were behind bot checks and were not read; the narration says so aloud, and the list marks the thinner ones.
